outcome: Soham Ghosh (University of Washington) posted a preprint in January 2025 claiming a complete proof of the Casas-Alvero conjecture for all degrees d>=3 over any characteristic-0 field, using Koszul homology; as of the March 2026 revision it remains an unreviewed preprint with no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification found. Separately, a genuinely peer-reviewed partial result (Schaub & Spivakovsky, Journal of Commutative Algebra, accepted January 2025) settled the conjecture's reformulated resultant-independence condition for the top three indices (i in {d-3, d-2, d-1}), and an earlier Ghosh preprint (Feb 2024) proved a finiteness result about the associated variety. No AI system was involved in any of this work.

disputes.summary: Ghosh's arXiv:2501.09272 claims a full resolution of the conjecture (confirming direction: every such polynomial is a d-th power of a linear polynomial) but has not been digested by experts as far as I could establish: it carries no journal acceptance, no cited independent verification, and was still being substantially revised (v1 15KB in Jan 2025 to v2 30KB in March 2026, described as 'major revisions') fourteen months after posting, which is itself a sign the argument was still being reworked rather than settled. Meanwhile the peer-reviewed Schaub-Spivakovsky paper only proves a restricted case (the top three resultant indices), leaving open whether Ghosh's broader claim is what actually closes the conjecture, a distinct result, or contains a gap the community has not yet flagged in searchable sources.

summary: Three distinct pieces of work touch this problem inside the window, none involving AI. (1) Soham Ghosh's arXiv:2501.09272 (submitted 2025-01-16, revised to v2 on 2026-03-21) claims a complete proof of the Casas-Alvero conjecture for every degree d>=3 over any characteristic-0 field, via Koszul homology and an analysis of 'almost counterexamples' using Brouwer degree techniques. I read the abstract and structure directly (fetched the PDF and abstract page); there is no acknowledgement of AI tool use, and no evidence the proof has been digested by an expert, accepted by a journal, or independently verified -- searches for retraction, error, or acceptance news turned up nothing, but the paper's own long gap between v1 and a 'major revision' v2 fourteen months later is itself evidence the argument was still being worked on, not settled. Given the standard here (resolved requires an expert digestion or journal acceptance; claimed is the right code for an unreviewed preprint however clean it looks), I classify this as claimed rather than resolved. (2) Independently, Daniel Schaub and Mark Spivakovsky published 'On the Casas-Alvero Conjecture' in the Journal of Commutative Algebra (received 2024-11-07, accepted 2025-01-12, published Summer 2025), a genuinely peer-reviewed result, but it only proves the reformulated resultant-independence condition for the top three indices i in {d-3, d-2, d-1} -- a partial case, not a full resolution. (3) Ghosh's earlier preprint arXiv:2402.18717 (submitted 2024-02-28) proved a finiteness result (the associated arithmetic Casas-Alvero scheme has finitely many rational points in any degree, and the variety is at most two-dimensional) -- also a partial, structural result predating and apparently feeding into the January 2025 full-proof claim. A later paper, arXiv:2608.14726 (Marashdeh, submitted 2026-08-12), gives further structural obstructions on any hypothetical counterexample (constraints on 'centred normal form', connections to MacMahon's determinant and 'bad primes') but explicitly does not claim to resolve the conjecture and does not reference Ghosh's work in the content I could access. I searched broadly for any AI system (LLM, AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, DeepMind formal-methods tools) touching this specific conjecture and found none; a 2025 'Gödel Test' LLM-conjecture benchmark and a 2026 'Formal Conjectures' verified-discovery benchmark were both checked directly and neither mentions Casas-Alvero.
competing_reading: One could argue the decisive event is the Schaub-Spivakovsky peer-reviewed partial result rather than Ghosh's unreviewed full-proof claim, since it is the only development in the window that has actually passed expert review, and under that reading status would be `partial` (direction confirmed, since the top-index cases matched the conjecture's prediction) rather than `claimed`. I chose `claimed` because Ghosh's paper, if correct, is a strictly larger event (full resolution vs. one case), and the rules ask for the decisive event the status rests on; but since I could not confirm expert acceptance of Ghosh's proof, a reader who weighs 'peer-reviewed but partial' above 'complete but unreviewed' would reasonably record this as `partial` instead.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from a specialist (a blog post, MathOverflow answer, or journal referee report) explicitly endorsing or rejecting Ghosh's Koszul-homology argument in arXiv:2501.09272, or a further arXiv revision/journal submission record showing acceptance, would settle whether `claimed` should become `resolved` (or be dropped if a flaw surfaces).

corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, WITH DOUBT. Scope is right: Ghosh claims the conjecture in every degree over any characteristic-0 field. Credibility is the open question. Against: the conjecture has a history of flawed claimed proofs, the preprint needed a 'major revision' fourteen months after posting, and no expert has engaged with it. For: the author is a working mathematician, the method (Koszul homology) is a serious one, and nothing has knocked it down. That is not enough to set it aside as the non-credible-claims batch did, where the problem would be a landmark and the claim came from outside the field, so it stays `claimed`. It is one of the rows a planned 'doubtful claim' marker is for.
